slides.title: A hit rate belongs to a trace and an initial state
keyPoints: The same addresses can behave differently when warm
Each access changes the state seen by the next
Name the cache level and observation interval
slides.narration: A cache trace is a story about changing state. An access may find a resident line, or it may bring a new block in and displace another. Starting cold is a specific assumption: no requested block is initially present. Starting with the final state of an earlier run can change the very first event. Therefore, a percentage without the access sequence and initial condition is incomplete evidence. We will separate rate arithmetic from state simulation, then compare the same trace under two placement rules. Both models are deterministic and useful for reasoning; neither measures elapsed cycles on a real processor.
actions: Ask for the trace, starting state, and denominator before opening the answer.

question.prompt: Why can repeating the same address list yield a different hit rate?
question.answer: The second run may begin with useful resident state retained from the first run instead of an empty cache.

slides.title: Keep local and global denominators separate
keyPoints: One thousand original accesses produce one hundred L1 misses
Twenty of those requests also miss L2
L2 local miss rate is 20%; global is 2%
slides.narration: The program prints three rates from explicit counts. One hundred of one thousand original accesses miss L1, giving ten percent. Twenty of the one hundred requests reaching L2 miss there, giving a local L2 rate of twenty percent. Those same twenty are only two percent of the original one thousand. The difference is the denominator, not contradictory data. Multiplying ten percent by twenty percent gives the global two percent; adding them would be wrong. These are supplied counts in an arithmetic example, not collected hardware events. A real report should state whether its counters include all original accesses or only requests reaching one level.

question.prompt: Why is ten percent plus twenty percent not the global miss rate?
question.answer: The twenty percent applies only to the subset that missed L1; the fractions must be multiplied, not added.

slides.title: A compulsory miss depends on the stated reference model
keyPoints: Cold first use brings in a previously unseen block
Prefetch can change observed demand behavior
Classification is not a permanent label on an address
slides.narration: In a cold model with no prefetch, the first request for a block must obtain it. That is a compulsory miss. The same numeric address is not forever labeled compulsory: a later request may hit, or it may miss after eviction for a different reason. Prefetching adds another distinction because data can arrive before its first demand access. The transfer still happened, but the first demand need not be a miss. Always state the initial state and whether the model includes prefetch. Otherwise two correct traces can appear to disagree simply because they answer different questions about when the block became resident.
actions: Ask for the trace, starting state, and denominator before opening the answer.

question.prompt: Can the first demand access hit when prefetching is included?
question.answer: Yes. Prefetch may already have installed the block, though obtaining its bytes still had a cost.

slides.title: Compare a conflict against equal-capacity flexible placement
keyPoints: Both model caches hold two blocks
Direct mapping makes blocks zero and two collide
A fully associative LRU reference retains both
slides.narration: The trace is block zero, block two, block zero, block two. In the two-slot direct-mapped model, both blocks select slot zero and keep evicting each other, so all four accesses miss. The fully associative reference also holds only two blocks, but it may place them in either slot. Its first two accesses miss and its final two hit. The output therefore reports zero direct hits and two reference hits. This comparison supports a conflict explanation for the repeated misses, not a total-capacity shortage. We use block numbers directly here, not byte addresses, and the list maintains most-recently-used order for the reference policy.
actions: Predict every printed value, run the model, then name its capacity, initial-state, and counting assumptions.

slides.title: Where the simple approach fails
keyPoints: Calling the second access to block 0 a compulsory miss is wrong. That block has been seen before; this eviction is a conflict relative to a four-line fully associative LRU reference.
A related failure in the generalized operation is concrete: Initialize unsigned slots to zero and compare only the stored value. The first access to block zero is incorrectly called a hit.
The repair changes the operation at the point where the rule can be enforced: Represent validity explicitly, with optional or a valid bit, and include block zero as the first cold access in a test.

slides.title: Compulsory misses
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A compulsory miss is the first access to a block in a cold-cache reference model.
The block has not yet been brought into the cache by a prior access in that model.
Larger lines can reduce the number of distinct blocks for a sequential region but can also fetch unused bytes.
Prefetching changes when a block is brought in and how demand misses are observed.

slides.title: Conflict misses
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A conflict miss arises from restricted placement in sets when a fully associative reference cache of the same capacity would have retained the block.
Repeated collisions can cause misses even when the total active block count is no greater than cache capacity.
The compulsory/capacity/conflict model is useful but incomplete for coherent multiprocessors.
Invalidations, sharing, prefetch interactions, and other effects can introduce additional causes.

slides.narration:
The following direct-mapped model has four lines of 16 bytes each. The trace accesses byte addresses 0, 16, 0, 64, 0, 16 . Blocks 0 and 4 both map to slot 0, while block 1 maps to slot 1. Companion listing: ch30/cache.py The output is M M H M M H , followed by hits=2 misses=4 . First references to blocks 0, 1, and 4 are compulsory misses. The later miss on block 0 is a conflict miss relative to a four-line fully associative LRU cache, which could retain all three blocks. The overall hit rate is 2/6 , approximately 33.3%. No cycle count follows from that percentage alone. A cost model is needed to translate the event sequence into a time estimate.

slides.title: Capacity classification needs the reference cache and policy
keyPoints: Too much active data can defeat any placement flexibility
The reference commonly uses fully associative LRU
Reuse distance helps explain what could remain resident
slides.narration: Now imagine a two-line fully associative LRU reference visiting blocks zero, one, two, then zero. The first three are new blocks. Installing two evicts zero under LRU, so the final zero misses even without set restrictions. That supports a capacity-related classification under this stated reference. It does not make zero inherently a capacity-miss address in every trace or replacement policy. Classification depends on history and the comparison model. A production processor can also have coherence invalidations and prefetch effects outside the simple three-category model. Use the model to explain a specific observation without forcing every hardware event into categories that omit its cause.
actions: Ask for the trace, starting state, and denominator before opening the answer.

question.prompt: Why must replacement policy be stated for a capacity reference trace?
question.answer: It determines which blocks remain after competing accesses and therefore whether the reference would hit on a later reuse.

slides.title: Observe the old state before installing the new block
keyPoints: Check hit against current residency
On a miss, replace only the selected slot
Explicit emptiness keeps block zero valid
slides.narration: The source lab uses optional values for slots. An empty optional means no block is resident, while a present optional can hold any unsigned block number, including zero. For each access, the function checks that old state first, then installs the requested block in the selected slot. Reversing these steps would make the new block appear to match itself and inflate the hit count. Other slots retain their state. The vector is local to the function, so each call starts cold by contract. If a later feature preserves the vector across calls, that intentionally changes the initial-state policy and needs new tests.

slides.title: A hit avoids some work, not all work
keyPoints: Lookup and delivery still cost resources
Dependencies can keep hit latency on the critical path
Writes may require additional permission work
slides.narration: A cache hit is not an operation that takes zero time. The processor still performs lookup, obtains the data, and uses it according to instruction dependencies. A long chain of dependent hits can limit progress even with a high hit rate. For writes on a coherent machine, a resident line may also require permission changes or communication before the store can proceed. The chapter’s simple model uses reads so residency and tag identity are enough for classification. Do not silently apply its hit definition to every write scenario. Name the operation and the modeled state before translating a hit count into a performance claim.
actions: Ask for the trace, starting state, and denominator before opening the answer.

question.prompt: Why can a read-only hit model be insufficient for analyzing writes?
question.answer: Writes may require ownership or coherence permissions beyond merely finding a resident tag.

slides.title: A percentage needs a cost model before it predicts time
keyPoints: Miss destinations have different costs
Independent misses may overlap
Critical-path events can dominate a high average hit rate
slides.narration: Suppose ninety-six percent of accesses hit. That percentage alone does not tell us whether the remaining four percent hit in the next cache, wait on main memory, overlap with other work, or stall a serial dependency chain. An average-cost formula must state its hit cost, miss penalty, and assumptions about overlap. Even then it is a model, not a substitute for a measurement under the actual workload. Report the exact counts as well as percentages for small traces: two hits among six accesses is easier to audit than a rounded thirty-three-point-three percent without its denominator.

slides.narration: The source hit-count helper deliberately creates a fresh slot vector on every call. Two calls with the same inputs therefore repeat the same cold trace. A persistent cache object would instead retain the final state until reset. Both APIs are reasonable, but they answer different questions. Tests should make that policy visible rather than relying on hidden static storage. For a persistent version, verify one cold pass, an immediate warm pass, and a pass after reset. When a benchmark warms up before measurement, document that too. Otherwise a performance comparison may merely compare different starting states rather than different implementations.

example.title: Trace hits before computing a hit rate
explain: The slot holds a complete block number in this small model. Equality means the requested block is already resident; -1 represents an empty slot.
Adding a Boolean adds one for true and zero for false. hits records observed hits before any replacement.
Install the requested block even on a miss. This can evict another block mapped to the same slot.
Print H for the previously observed hit, M otherwise. Testing after installation would falsely turn every access into a hit.
example.invariant: Hit detection uses the resident state before the access installs a block. Empty slots cannot match a valid request.
example.output: M M H M M H hits=2
